The property's forecast net property income (“NPI”) for CY2026 remains on track, and the refinancing

million in all-in debt costs. In addition, the reconfiguration of approximately 16,000 sq ft of retail space

commitments secured for two of the five units, in line with expectations. We look forward to announcing 
the incoming tenants, including new-to-market concepts, in due course. 
Upon completion of the reconfiguration works and stabilisation of the new tenancies, the Manager 
expects the reconfigured space to achieve an uplift in rental income and generate an estimated rental 
reversion of approximately two times the existing rental.

productivity of the mall's retail space to support sustainable income growth over the long term.

Question: The reported average cost of debt excludes amortisation of debt-related transaction 
costs (and other fees). What is the all-in weighted average cost of debt? When evaluating 
refinancing, new debt or other funding options, does the manager assess funding costs on an 
all-in basis, including transaction costs, fees and other financing-related expenses? 
The weighted average cost of debt reported in Lendlease REIT's FY2026 financial statements at 
2.75% represents the average rate for the financial year FY2026.  It comprises the interest margins 
charged by the banks for the respective loan facilities on top of the base interest costs. Base interest 
costs are dependent on market interest rates, subject to locking in fixed rates via interest rate hedges.  
Lendlease REIT has hedged 68% of its interest exposure as at 30 June 2026. 
The weighted average cost of debt excludes the amortisation of debt-related transaction costs, which 
are the upfront fees charged by the lenders at the establishment of each facility. Such fees are 
capitalized and amortized over the tenure of the relevant facilities in accordance with applicable 
accounting standards. Due to confidentiality of the commercial arrangements with the banks, we are 
unable to disclose the level of these fees and therefore the all-in weighted average cost of debt (adding 
on these fees). We would like to highlight that the amortization of upfront fees does not impact the 
distributable income.      
When evaluating debt funding and refinancing opportunities, the Manager considers a range of 
factors, including the interest margin and the upfront fee charged by the banks (i.e. together the all-in 
rate), debt tenor, liquidity and lender diversification.

of product quality, competitive pricing, delivery reliability, logistics capabilities and 
established customer relationships, rather than price alone. Repeat orders from an

contracts with better margins rather than competing on price.

industry since 2015, spanning more than a decade, and has developed a strong 
understanding of clients’ technical requirements, operational expectations and project

advantages, as offshore and marine clients generally prefer proven suppliers. In 
addition, as the Group also provides transport, security and manpower services, it often 
has existing relationships with clients across more than one business segment. These 
touch points give the Group a better understanding of clients’ wider operational needs 
and allow it to offer complementary services alongside grating supply. Having said that, 
the market is competitive, and these advantages must be sustained through continued 
operational performance, strong supplier relationships and competitive pricing. The

were served largely with the existing fleet, together with continued fleet optimisation, 
better route planning and stronger demand from commercial clients. As a result, 
revenue grew faster than the segment’s main operating costs. Driver salaries and 
related costs increased by about 12.4%, while repair and maintenance and insurance 
costs increased by about 2.4% and 2.6% respectively. Depreciation decreased by 
about $137,000, as more of the fleet became fully depreciated while remaining in 
service.

services, with subcontractor costs increasing from about $0.86 million to $1.79 million.

grew by 26.4%, below revenue growth of 31.8%, resulting in the higher gross margin.

utilisation, pricing and changes in customer or service mix operate together and are 
not tracked separately in a way that allows their respective contributions to be reliably 
quantified. Diesel cost remains a key sensitivity, and the Group takes fuel prices into 
account when pricing new and renewed contracts. The Group will continue to focus on 
securing contracts with healthy margins and managing operating costs prudently.

promptly while it assesses whether their volume and duration justify further investment

scopes and peak workloads, and to manpower services, for peak-period deployment.

fixed costs ahead of demand.

margin improved from 37.6% to 40.7%. The improvement was driven mainly by stronger margins in the

Q1 (i) How is the group securing projects in these newer end-markets, and what role does it play in 
the project value chain? Specifically, what proportion of these projects is contracted directly with 
end-users or project owners, rather than through main contractors or engineering, procurement 
and construction contractors? 
 
Company’s Response:  
 
The Group secures work in data centre, semiconductor and biopharmaceutical projects on the same basis 
as in its established markets: its track record in complex, safety-critical lifting, the breadth of its fleet and 
its ability to mobilise equipment and people at short notice. Many of these developments are fast-track 
projects, where customers place as much weight on reliability, safety and execution certainty as on price. 
Several of these customers have worked with the Group before, and it aims to carry its work into later 
phases of their developments. 
 
In the project value chain, the Group provides heavy lifting, heavy haulage, marine transportation and 
installation services. Its scope ranges from the hire of cranes with operators to integrated packages 
covering lift engineering and planning, transport, installation and skidding. In the data centre sector, for 
example, the Group has moved from supplying cranes and transport on a rental basis to offering integrated 
lifting, transport and module installation packages. 

2 
 
In these newer end-markets, the Group is contracted by main contractors and engineering, procurement 
and construction (“EPC”) contractors rather than directly by project owners. Across its business as a whole, 
the Group works both directly with project owners and as a subcontractor, with the majority of its work 
contracted through main contractors. Which route applies is generally determined by the project owner’s 
procurement model.  
 
Q1 (ii) What proportion of the group’s revenue and gross profit is generated by equipment rental 
alone, compared with integrated solutions that may include engineering, project management, 
haulage and other value-added services? Given the greater operational complexity and execution 
risks, what safeguard does management have in place to manage potential liabilities, including 
those arising from unexpected operational mishaps? 
 
Company’s Response: 
 
Note 4 to the financial statements analyses FY2026 revenue by type: rental income of $142.6 million (76% 
of Group revenue), revenue from the rendering of services of $39.6 million (21%) and trading sales of 
equipment and spare parts of $5.4 million (3%). Rental income arises from the hire of machinery with the 
operating manpower integral to the hire. Services revenue arises from projects involving value-added 
logistics and engineering activities. 
 
This classification does not correspond exactly to the distinction between equipment rental alone and 
integrated solutions. An integrated project usually generates both rental income, for the equipment and 
crews deployed, and services revenue, for the engineering, transport and installation work. Integrated 
projects generally earn higher margins than rental-only work, reflecting their engineering content and 
execution risk. 
 
Integrated work carries greater operational complexity, and the Group manages the associated risks at 
several levels: 
 
 
Engineering and project control: each stage of a project, from site surveys, planning and scheduling 
to equipment deployment, logistics and execution, is planned, reviewed and monitored by experienced 
engineers, foremen and supervisors, and the Executive Directors and key management oversee major 
projects. Fixed-price work is subject to cost monitoring and control procedures. 
 
 
Safety management: the Group’s occupational health and safety management system is supported by 
ISO 45001:2018 and ISO 9001:2015 certification, and by bizSAFE Star certification for its Singapore 
operations. Risk assessments, job safety analyses and inspections cover lifting and transport activities, 
and every worker has the authority to refuse unsafe work. Management visits work sites regularly to 
review safety performance and behaviour, and the well-being of its teams. There were no fatalities or 
high-consequence work-related injuries in FY2024, FY2025 or FY2026, and the rate of recordable work-
related injuries fell to 2.3 per million hours worked in FY2026, from 3.6 in FY2025. 
 
 
Equipment: the fleet is kept under regular maintenance programmes and renewed periodically, with 
stringent equipment quality controls. 
 
 
Contracts and insurance: contractual liabilities, indemnities and insurance requirements are reviewed 
for each project according to its risks and contractual obligations. 
 
 
Oversight: the Enterprise Risk Management Committee, a sub-committee of the Audit Committee, 
assesses identified risks and records them in the Group’s risk register, which it reviews periodically. 
 

3 
 
During the year, the group invested $53.5 million in property, plant and equipment to renew and 
expand its fleet, extend its lifting range and undertake larger and more technically demanding 
projects. 
 
Q1 (iii) With average heavy lifting asset utilisation at 57%, how does management identify the 
specific equipment classes and markets where additional capacity is justified? What investment 
hurdle rates does the board apply when approving new equipment purchases?  
 
Company’s Response: 
 
The average utilisation rate of 57% (FY2025: 54%) is a fleet-level figure across more than 600 cranes of 
very different types and capacities, from lorry cranes to the Group’s 2,200-tonne crawler crane, and it varies 
with mobilisation schedules, capacity limits, location and other operational factors. Management therefore 
assesses utilisation and returns by asset and by market rather than at fleet level. One large crane that is 
well utilised can contribute more than many smaller units with spare capacity. 
 
In deciding where additional capacity is justified, management considers: 
 
 
Cross-hire: where the Group repeatedly hires equipment from third parties to meet demand in a 
particular class, this points to a capacity gap. Cross-hire costs were elevated in FY2025 and FY2026, 
reflecting the strength of demand. In FY2026, overlapping project timelines also required the Group to 
hire in equipment to meet customers’ schedules and avoid delays. Some cross-hire is a normal part of 
the business, allowing the Group to take on work beyond its own fleet at any one time. 
 
 
Pipeline and customer requirements: the projects being tendered, particularly those requiring 
integrated solutions, where customers look for an asset-backed provider able to commit the equipment 
needed. 
 
 
Market capacity: in some size classes the market already has ample capacity and hiring in is more 
economical than owning. The Group concentrates its own investment on specialised and higher-capacity 
equipment. 
 
 
Fleet renewal: the fleet is renewed on a rolling basis as equipment reaches the end of its working life, 
and part of each year’s capital expenditure replaces older units. 
 
The Group also recycles capital, divesting underutilised units and redeploying the capital released. In 
FY2026, investment in property, plant and equipment of $53.5 million compared with a depreciation charge 
of $35.7 million. 
 
Proposals for new equipment are evaluated on their expected returns, cash flows and utilisation, and on 
downside scenarios, against the Group’s cost of capital. Return on equity has improved in each of the past 
four years, from 4.0% in FY2022 to 7.0% in FY2026.

The Building and Construction Authority projects total construction demand of $47 billion to $53 billion in 
2026 and $39 billion to $46 billion a year from 2027 to 2030, anchored by major projects such as Changi 
Airport Terminal 5. Over the longer term, the plans announced at the National Day Rally in August 2026 to

connect several smaller islands south of Jurong Island into a new western island may create further

pipeline. Project activity can nonetheless vary from year to year, depending on the timing of contract awards 
and construction schedules. 
 
The business is nonetheless cyclical, and the Group has been through a severe downturn before. That 
experience shapes how the Group is run today: 
 
 
Balance sheet: as at 30 June 2026 the Group had cash and bank deposits of $86.6 million, net gearing 
of 9.5% and shareholders’ funds of $341.6 million. 
 
 
Diversification: the Group serves more than 300 customers a month across a range of sectors and 
markets, and no single customer accounted for more than 10% of revenue in FY2026. Contracted project 
work accounts for less than half of revenue, so the Group is not locked into long-term contracts priced 
on assumptions that may no longer hold. 
 
 
Flexibility: capital expenditure can be deferred, cross-hired equipment released and owned equipment 
redeployed across the Group’s markets as conditions change. 
 
While the Board does not conduct a separate formal stress test, the Group’s resilience is monitored through 
its financial planning and control processes, which are reported to the Board and include: 
 
 
Annual budgeting: the Group prepares an annual budget setting out its financial plan for the year. 
 
 
Variance analysis: actual results are compared with the budget periodically, and significant variances 
are reviewed. 
 
 
Forecasting: forecasts are updated periodically during the year to reflect changes in market conditions. 
Where forecasts fall below budget, management can respond, for example by deferring capital 
expenditure. 
 
 
Fleet utilisation: the Board reviews fleet utilisation quarterly against internal targets. 
 
 
Capital expenditure: major capital expenditure is reviewed against forecast cash flows and available 
funding before it is approved. 
 
 
Liquidity and capital structure: operating cash flows and liquidity are monitored closely, adequate 
cash and bank deposits are maintained, and the capital structure and gearing are reviewed regularly. 
Headroom under banking facilities and compliance with loan covenants are also monitored. 
 
 
Credit control: customers are subject to credit reviews and credit limits and, where practicable, those 
of lower credit standing transact on cash terms or make advance payments. 
 
The Enterprise Risk Management Committee, overseen by the Audit Committee, monitors market and 
business risks, and the Board receives assurance each year on the adequacy and effectiveness of the 
Group’s risk management and internal control systems. In FY2025, the Group also performed its first 
climate scenario analysis under IFRS S2, which considered the transition risks under a below-2°C

Company’s Response: 
 
The Group joined Enterprise Singapore’s Scale-Up programme during FY2026. The programme runs in 
two phases, a strategy phase followed by an acceleration phase. The Group is now in the acceleration 
phase, which is expected to be completed around the end of 2026. Through the programme, management

supported by the respective operating business units, and fleet operations, safety and procurement 
managed at Group level; and

Group’s core capabilities, including opportunities that strengthen the Group’s position outside

these reflect external constraints, such as competition and market access, versus internal 
limitations in management bandwidth, local capabilities or willingness and ability to commit 
capital? At this stage of the group’s growth, how critical is regional expansion to its longer-term 
growth prospects?  
 
Company’s Response: 
 
Regional expansion is important to the Group’s long-term growth. Singapore remains the core market, 
where the Group’s fleet, engineering depth and customer relationships are greatest, but it is a relatively 
small market. The Group sees its overseas markets as a second engine of growth, extending its 
addressable market and diversifying its earnings. 
 
Singapore’s share of revenue rose to 77% in FY2026, from 73% in FY2025, mainly because Singapore 
revenue grew by $25.6 million on strong demand. Overseas revenue was $43.0 million, against $44.4 
million in FY2025: growth in India and Brunei was offset mainly by lower revenue from Malaysia, where a 
large one-off project in FY2025 was not repeated, and from the Middle East, where the pace of project 
execution moderated amid regional tensions. 
 
The constraints on building a larger overseas presence are both external and internal: 
 
 
External: heavy lifting is a local business in each market, with established local competitors, pricing 
pressure and local regulatory and licensing requirements. Project demand is uneven and, in some 
markets, exposed to political and geopolitical developments. The strength of the Singapore dollar has 
also given rise to foreign exchange losses, mainly on the intercompany balances through which 
overseas operations are funded; the Group’s net currency exchange loss was $3.9 million in FY2026. 
 
 
Internal: equipment can be moved between markets, but experienced people cannot be moved as 
easily. The main internal constraints are the availability of experienced local management and technical 
personnel, and the need to balance capital and equipment deployment between Singapore and the 
overseas markets. Building local teams that meet the Group’s safety and execution standards takes 
time. The new operating model described in (i) above is intended to strengthen Group-wide coordination 
and international business development capabilities.

capacity lifts, where its fleet and expertise give it an advantage, rather than on the mass market. It has

Mammoet in Thailand in 2023 to extend its capabilities there, and in August 2026 incorporated a subsidiary

Company’s response 
 
The Group’s Maintenance and Leasing Business comprises maintenance support services, leasing 
services and recurring technology-based security solutions services. Contracts for maintenance support 
services typically range from one to five years, while lease-and-maintenance contracts are generally 
entered into for a period of at least seven years. Please refer to page 16 of the Annual Report for an 
introduction to the Group’s Maintenance and Leasing Business.  
 
The revenue of the Maintenance and Leasing Business segment is largely supported by a key ongoing 
contract with a government agency in Southeast Asia for the provision of integrated security solutions 
which includes system implementation, support services as well as seven years of maintenance 
services following the completion of the implementation of each system. Please refer to the Company’s 
announcements dated 15 January 2019 and 9 January 2020 for details of this project. Save as 
disclosed, there are no other material ongoing projects under the Maintenance and Leasing Business 
segment.

is unable to disclose further details on the abovementioned contract and ongoing tender discussions.

approximately 7.7% of the Group’s total revenue was considered recurring revenue.

insurance policies taken up by the Group taking into account its contractual obligations, project scope

include the relevant Group entity and the customer as insured parties or additional insureds). The 
coverage of such insurance policies will be subject to the terms, limits and exclusions of the respective 
policies.

the review of customer requirements, solution design, product selection, procurement, system 
configuration, installation coordination, testing and commissioning, customer training and handover;

enterprise risk management framework.

the view that internal controls and risk management systems, including the abovementioned safeguards 
against potential financial exposure and operational risks, were adequate and effective as at the date 
of the Annual Report

qa.answer:
Q1. With the cessation of its UK operations, the group now operates in the key geographical 
markets of Australia and New Zealand. Through Pafu and Homm, the group has also expanded 
to Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia and Vietnam via sub-franchised and sub-licensed outlets. 
 
 
 
(Source: company annual report)  
 
Despite a reduction in Australian outlets from 136 to 131, revenue increased by 5.5% to 
$51.8 million. In New Zealand, outlet numbers increased from 37 to 38, yet revenue fell by 
8.2% to $12.3 million. 
 
(i) 
How do Australia and New Zealand differ in terms of market size, competitive intensity, 
consumer demand, pricing power and growth prospects? Which market offers the 
stronger prospects for profitable growth over the next three to five years, and what 
evidence supports management’s assessment? 
 
Response: 
 
Australia and New Zealand differ significantly in market size and growth opportunities. Australia 
has a substantially larger population, generally providing a larger market and greater 
opportunities for expansion across multiple urban centres. Whilst both markets are competitive 
and mature, the opportunities in Australia are more diverse. Its larger consumer base and wider 
geographical reach provide the Group with greater opportunities to expand its brand portfolio, 

2 
 
reach new customers and strengthen its market presence. Considering amongst others, the 
above factors, the Group focuses more of its resources to support its geographical presence in 
Australia. Focusing a stronger presence in a particular geographical market allows the Group a 
greater potential for central kitchen economies of scale. A broader brand portfolio also provides 
greater opportunities for expansion and reduces reliance on any single brand segment. 
 
The Group operates 12 brands and 131 outlets in Australia across various segments, compared 
with 4 brands and 38 outlets in New Zealand, of which 32 of them are Gong Cha outlets.  
 
Management will continue to pursue sustainable growth in both markets utilising a different 
strategy for each market, with a focus on operational efficiency, profitability and long-term value 
creation. 
 
 
(ii) 
How does management allocate capital between the two markets? How do company-
owned outlets in Australia and New Zealand compare in terms of sales growth, outlet-level 
profitability and returns on invested capital?    
 
Response: 
 
Please refer to the Company’s response in Q1(i) above. In FY2026, the Group’s capital allocation 
was weighted towards Australia, where majority of new outlet openings and brand launches took 
place, in line with the Group’s strategy in Australia. The Group’s strategy for New Zealand 
focuses more on selected brands. 
 
Revenue from company-owned outlets indicated stronger sales performance in Australia and 
softer performance in New Zealand resulting a better profitability and higher ROI in Australia than 
New Zealand. 
 
The Group remains open to explore suitable growth opportunities in both markets. Future capital 
allocation continues to be guided by amongst others, market conditions, outlet-level profitability 
and expected investment returns, with expansion pursued selectively to support sustainable 
growth and attractive returns. 
 
 
Profit attributable to equity holders of the company decreased from A$498,061 to 
A$150,784 in FY2026. 
 
(iii) 
What are management’s three highest-priority actions to restore profitability, and what 
quantified improvements in revenue, margins or operating costs is each expected to 
deliver?   
 
Response: 
 
The Group constantly seeks to remain competitive amidst challenges to deliver sustainable long-
term growth. Amongst others, Management will prioritise the following in implementing its 
strategic initiatives: 
 
1) Improve outlet performance and optimise the brand portfolio: Review existing outlets 
and the various operating models to assess how outlet performance may be improved. New 
outlet openings will be assessed based on their commercial viability and expected returns. 
 
2) Strengthen gross margins: Review menu offerings of various brands and outlets to assess 
adjustments that may strengthen gross margins, whilst remaining competitive. At the same 
time, to review procurement methods, including proactively sourcing for more competitive 
suppliers to manage procurement costs and counter mounting cost pressures.  
 

3 
 
3) Improve operational efficiency and manage overheads: Review kitchen and outlet 
operations for operational efficiency, including considering management of staffing and 
inventories. The Group will monitor key operating metrics regularly to identify inefficiencies 
and improve cost discipline across its operations. 
 
The potential improvements will be assessed with reference to historical performance, adapted 
to changing market environments for changes in operating conditions. Key indicators include 
outlet sales growth, gross profit margins, labour and food costs as a percentage of revenue, and 
overall operating profitability, with the objective of improving revenue performance, strengthening 
margins and enhancing cost efficiency

Would the board and management provide greater clarity on certain operational matters? 
Specifically: 
 
(i) 
New brands: The group opened its first TamJai Mixian outlet in Melbourne’s central business 
district in November 2024. In March 2025, it launched Onimusubi, a Japanese-style flavoured 
rice ball concept, opening its first outlet in Chadstone, a major shopping centre in Melbourne. 
Since then, two additional TamJai outlets have opened, one company-owned and one operated 
under a sub-franchise or sub-licensing arrangement, while the number of Onimusubi outlets 
has remained at one. What objective criteria does it use to determine whether a new 
concept has achieved product-market fit and is ready to scale?  
Conversely, what performance thresholds and review periods trigger changes to the 
menu, pricing or operating model, or a decision to discontinue the concept? 
 
Response: 
 
The Group adopts different development approaches for TamJai Mixian and Onimusubi, 
reflecting their respective brand maturity and track records. 
 
(a) Criteria for product-market fit and readiness to scale 
 
TamJai Mixian is an established Hong Kong brand founded in 1996, with more than 200 
outlets in Hong Kong. In 2024, the Group formed a majority-owned joint venture with 
TamJai International to develop the brand in Australia. Its first Melbourne CBD outlet 
opened in November 2024, followed by two additional outlets, one company-owned and 
one operated under a sub-franchise or sub-licensing arrangement. 
 
Onimusubi, a Japanese-style flavoured rice ball concept developed by the Group, launched 
its first outlet at Chadstone in March 2025 and currently operates at one location. 
 
In assessing whether a concept has achieved product-market fit and is ready to scale, the 
Group considers amongst others, outlet-level profitability, the replicability of the operating 
model and market conditions. TamJai Mixian benefits from an established overseas track 
record and brand recognition, which may facilitate expansion through sub-franchising or 
sub-licensing. Onimusubi remains at an earlier stage of development, requiring further 
assessment before broader expansion. 
 
(b) Performance reviews and corrective actions 
 
Please refer to the Company’s response in Q1(iii). The Group regularly reviews the existing 
operations and makes adjustments as it deems necessary. Its pricing and operating 
approach may be adjusted in response to significant changes in cost pressures, consumer 
preferences or market conditions. 
 

4 
 
The Group also monitors changes in applicable laws and regulations and will make the 
necessary adjustments to ensure compliance and maintain operational viability. 
 
(ii) 
Homm: How has the brand performed in Singapore against its original business case in 
terms of sales, outlet-level profitability and customer demand? What were the principal 
reasons for closing its Raffles City outlet after two years of operations? 
 
Response: 
 
Homm’s performance in Singapore was slightly below the original sales forecasts. While 
customer demand was present, sales patterns did not fully align with initial expectations. 
 
The Raffles City outlet was operated by a sub-franchisee. The sub-franchisee made the decision 
independently to close the outlet following its own review of performance and business outlook.  
 
(iii) 
Gong Cha: How does the brand maintain its competitive position amid competition from 
Chinese tea and beverage brands such as HEYTEA, CHAGEE, Molly Tea and Mixue? 
Separately, what implications, if any, does the change in ownership of Gong Cha’s brand 
intellectual property have for the group’s franchise or licensing rights, royalty obligations, 
operating costs and long-term ability to develop the brand? 
 
Response: 
 
The Group currently operates Gong Cha in New Zealand, with a total of 12 company-owned 
outlets and 20 sub-franchisee outlets. The Group monitors competition from both established 
bubble tea operators and emerging international tea and beverage brands. Whilst Chinese tea 
and beverage brands such as HEYTEA, CHAGEE, Molly Tea and Mixue continue to expand into 
overseas markets, the competitive landscape in New Zealand remains subject to ongoing 
developments. 
 
To maintain Gong Cha’s competitive position, the Group regularly refreshes its product offering 
and runs targeted marketing activities to strengthen brand awareness, retain existing customers 
and attract new customers. 
 
The change in Gong Cha’s brand ownership has not had a significant impact on the Group’s 
franchise rights and arrangements. The Group will continue to monitor the situation closely to 
ensure stability and long-term growth of the brand

The company has outsourced its internal audit function to CLA Global TS Holdings Pte. Ltd.   
 
(i) 
Is the joint venture operating the Maita supermarket business included within the scope 
of the group’s internal audit function? If not, how does the board obtain independent 
assurance over the joint venture’s financial controls, risk management and compliance, 
and what alternative assurance arrangements are in place? 
 
Response: 
 
The Maita supermarket business is operated through TST (Aust) Pty Ltd and its subsidiaries, a 
50:50 joint venture between the Group and its joint venture partner. As the joint venture is 
independently governed and accounted for using the equity method, it is not included within the 
scope of the Group’s internal audit function. 
 
The Group oversees the finance function of the joint venture, while the other shareholder 
oversees its operational functions. Certain key matters are subject to joint approval, providing a 

5 
 
governance mechanism for both shareholders to oversee key decisions and the joint venture’s 
operations. 
 
The financial statements of TST (Aust) Pty Ltd and its subsidiaries are subject to independent 
external audit. The Group considers that the existing governance arrangements, segregation of 
responsibilities and joint approval mechanisms and independent external audit provide 
appropriate oversight over the joint venture. The Group will continue to monitor the adequacy of 
these arrangements and assess whether additional assurance measures are required where 
appropriate. 
 
(ii) 
Given that the group’s operations are primarily in Australia and New Zealand, while its 
outsourced internal audit provider appears to be the Singapore-based entity, could the 
company clarify how internal audits are conducted on the ground? Are the audits 
performed by Singapore-based personnel, local teams in Australia and New Zealand, or a 
combination of both?   
 
Response: 
The Group’s internal audits are conducted by Singapore-based personnel from a Singapore-
based outsourced internal audit provider. While there is no local internal audit team based in 
Australia or New Zealand, the audit approach includes on-site fieldwork to Australia and New 
Zealand depending on the scope and nature of the audit, to review the relevant operational 
processes and internal controls.  Accordingly, the internal audit team adopts a combination of 
Singapore-based audit planning and oversight, together with on-site fieldwork in Australia and 
New Zealand. 
(iii) 
How does the IA bridge any gaps in local knowledge of Australia and New Zealand, where 
regulatory requirements, business practices and workplace cultures may differ from 
Singapore, while meeting the internal audit standards and governance expectations 
applicable to an SGX-listed company? 
 
Response: 
 
The IA team is based in Singapore and undertakes the necessary research and familiarisation 
with the relevant laws, regulations and business practices applicable to the Group’s operations 
in Australia and New Zealand. The team also engages with local management to understand the 
local operating environment and, where necessary, seeks input from relevant subject matter 
experts to validate its understanding of applicable requirements. 
 
All reviews are conducted using a consistent risk-based internal audit methodology aligned with 
the International Standards for the Professional Practice of Internal Auditing and the governance 
expectations of an SGX-listed company. This includes assessing the adequacy and effectiveness 
of internal controls, risk management processes and compliance frameworks, while taking into 
consideration both SGX governance requirements and local regulatory obligations. 
 
(iv) 
What was the scope of the internal audit in FY2026 and what were the key findings? 
 
Response: 
 
The FY2026 internal audit covered three outlets in Australia and New Zealand and reviewed key 
business processes, including Sales to Collection, Procurement, Payables and Payment, Fixed 
Assets and Inventory Management, Human Resources and Payroll, together with an internal 
review of selected environmental, social and governance (“ESG”) matters. 
The review identified Moderate-risk and Low-risk findings, with no High-risk findings identified.
